note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Begin with the exact-species attached flowering head (panel 11) and the tiered whorl/junction views (panels 3 and 5). On the flowering axis identify the repeatedly spaced sets of long slender one-sided racemes and terminal upright branch, not only a detached tumble head. Published species description gives about 10–16 racemes 5–15 cm long, but those numbers are not photographic measurements. Compare the compact single terminal fan of DIFFERENT species feather fingergrass (panel 16) rather than mixing the two plants' spikelets. The actual crown/root close-up is in panel 6 but not on the same continuous flowering culm specimen.
tiles.short: Long one-sided racemes in separated tiers
tiles.status: ACTUAL TIERED ATTACHED FLOWERING AXIS PICTURED; SINGLE ROOT-TO-HEAD CONTINUOUS VOUCHER NOT SHOWN

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTS AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Panel 6 is a REAL pulled-up exact-species fibrous-root crown with flattened basal tillers and bent lower culms. That verifies the rooted perennial growth form, but does not demonstrate roots at a separate spreading NODE or a same-voucher whole flowering plant. Panels 7, 8 and 12 show the external blade–sheath junction; new exact-species San Antonio panel 15 adds a living green blade insertion and pale outer sheath rim. The true INSIDE short 0.7–1.3 mm ciliate membranous ligule has NOT been physically opened or measured with a ruler in any of these photographs; nearby pale collar hairs are not proof of membrane height. Panel 13 shows a stem node: it is NOT the inner leaf ligule. Do not infer rhizomes or rooted stolons unless visibly connected on a real specimen.
tiles.short: Perennial fibrous tuft; lower nodes may root
tiles.status: TRUE FIBROUS ROOTED CROWN AND EXTERIOR COLLARS PHOTO-VERIFIED; EXACT 1-MM INNER LIGULE AND SECONDARY ROOTING NODES MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · ONE SPIKELET, TWO FLORETS
tiles.details: A single mature Chloris verticillata spikelet contains a lower fertile (bisexual) and an upper sterile floret, surrounded by two basal glumes. New actual same-species Douglas Goldman close panel 14 follows the attached ONE-SIDED narrow rachis and its overlapping small spikelet units; existing panels 1, 2, 4 and 9 capture awned mature details. Individual glumes and paired lower/upper lemmas cannot be safely separated from these images. Spikelet body length about 2–3.5 mm EXCLUDES the much longer awns; please use a true 0.5–1-mm ruler when dissecting rather than a finger for scale.
tiles.short: Awns excluded from the spikelet-body length
tiles.status: REAL ATTACHED SPIKELET SEQUENCE AND AWNED MACROS PRESENT; BOTH FLORETS MUST BE DISSECTED WITH SCALE

tiles.heading: 04 · FIND BOTH GLUMES
tiles.details: Lower and upper glumes are distinct outer basal bracts, separate from the fertile and sterile lemmas. The source FNA treatment reports lower glume 2–3 mm and upper glume 2.8–3.5 mm. New panel 14 illustrates the true arrangement of overlapping awned units on ONE intact raceme but does not isolate a measurable glume pair. Hold the diagnostic measurement until a same-voucher mature spikelet is physically taken apart, placed glumes separately on a scale, and their structures are backlit. A glume does NOT produce either of the two long lemma awns.
tiles.status: LIVE ATTACHED SPIKELETS NOW CLOSER; LOWER / UPPER GLUMES STILL UNSEPARATED AND UNMEASURED

tiles.heading: 05 · TRACE TWO DIFFERENT AWNS
tiles.details: Long awns are genuinely visible on source-identified tumble windmillgrass in panels 1, 2, 4, 10 and 14. Published FNA gives the lower fertile lemma awn ~4.8–9 mm and the upper sterile lemma awn ~3.2–7 mm, measured separately. The current photographs DO NOT show continuous awn attachment to each individual dissected lemma: do not label a visible awn as 'fertile' or 'sterile' based only on its position against overlapped spikelets. For contrast, panel 17 is genuine Chloris virgata (a DIFFERENT species) with conspicuous longer white apical hair crown; never use those other-species hairs as tumble lemma proof.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma awn ≈4.8–9 mm; sterile ≈3.2–7 mm
tiles.status: ACTUAL AWNS PRESENT; SEPARATE FERTILE/STERILE LEMMA ATTACHMENTS AND MILLIMETER LENGTH NOT CERTIFIED

tiles.heading: 06 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKE CHECK
tiles.details: Three distinct grasses now have local credited visual comparisons: C. verticillata (actual long racemes in tiered whorls, panels 11/3), C. cucullata (shorter crowded whorls, panel 0; the left unrelated dense plume in that photograph is not target anatomy), and C. virgata (compact terminal feathery fan, panel 16, and a distinctive long-haired floret crown, panel 17). These C. virgata images are OTHER-species photos, not evidence of tumble windmillgrass organs. Hooded C. cucullata requires isolation of a swollen UPPER STERILE lemma, distinct from its basal UPPER GLUME. Hybrid C. × subdolichostachya cannot be confirmed from tier spacing alone; matched measured mature florets are required.
tiles.short: Hooded vs tumble: glume ≠ sterile hood
tiles.status: C. CUCULLATA AND C. VIRGATA LOOK-ALIKE GALLERIES LOCAL AND LABELED; HYBRID/MATURE FLORET DISSECTION HOLD

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Look for LONG racemes arising in DISTINCT tiers or whorls along a flowering stem, sometimes with an upright terminal branch. The panicle can detach and tumble, but that fact and the head silhouette alone are not enough: mature spikelets should have longer awns than hooded windmillgrass, with fertile lemma awn around 4.8–9 mm and sterile lemma awn around 3.2–7 mm.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Perennial windmillgrass with ~10–16 racemes in separated whorls; ripe panicle may detach and tumble.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Panel 6 is a REAL pulled-up exact-species fibrous-root crown with flattened basal tillers and bent lower culms. That verifies the rooted perennial growth form, but does not demonstrate roots at a separate spreading NODE or a same-voucher whole flowering plant. Panels 7, 8 and 12 show the external blade–sheath junction; new exact-species San Antonio panel 15 adds a living green blade insertion and pale outer sheath rim. The true INSIDE short 0.7–1.3 mm ciliate membranous ligule has NOT been physically opened or measured with a ruler in any of these photographs; nearby pale collar hairs are not proof of membrane height. Panel 13 shows a stem node: it is NOT the inner leaf ligule. Do not infer rhizomes or rooted stolons unless visibly connected on a real specimen.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Fertile lemma awn ~4.8–9 mm; sterile lemma awn ~3.2–7 mm. Upper sterile floret is not a conspicuously swollen round hood.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Tumble windmillgrass tends to have separated tiers of longer (~5–15 cm) racemes and long awns. C. cucullata tends to have crowded shorter whorls and a swollen short-awned sterile hood. C. virgata often has one terminal feathery fan and a different fertile-lemma hair crown. The hybrid between cucullata and verticillata is a real confounder: never certify hybrid status from tier spacing.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE: FEATHER FINGERGRASS — compact terminal fan, not separated tumble whorls
panels.caption: This is Chloris virgata, a DIFFERENT grass photographed by Matt Lavin, not tumble windmillgrass. It typically places its racemes close together in one feathery terminal fan, unlike the separately spaced tiers on the flowering axis of C. verticillata. Gross head architecture is a first clue, never proof by itself. Compare its special long floret hair crown in the next panel.

The conspicuous whitish apical hair crown and projecting awns are REAL structures on this DIFFERENT species. Do NOT borrow these long hairs to annotate the subtler tumble windmillgrass floret or claim these are separate fertile and sterile tumble lemma awns. Dissect one source-vouchered mature floret to finish a species ID.

intro: Look for LONG racemes arising in DISTINCT tiers or whorls along a flowering stem, sometimes with an upright terminal branch. The panicle can detach and tumble, but that fact and the head silhouette alone are not enough: mature spikelets should have longer awns than hooded windmillgrass, with fertile lemma awn around 4.8–9 mm and sterile lemma awn around 3.2–7 mm.
memory_rule: On an intact stalk, photograph the entire head from the lowest tier to highest; see whether rays attach at different heights.
safety_note: Thirteen existing source records are physically archived (12 photographs, 1 historical USDA illustration), but only six selected images are featured in this quickcheck. The 11-panel comparison gallery remains unchanged except one verified collar-hair arrow. Photo indices are zero-based images[] entries. Do not claim measured glume/lemma/ligule anatomy or 100% completion from these photos; Joey CC BY-NC files remain noncommercial-use conditional.
field_rule: Tumble windmillgrass tends to have separated tiers of longer (~5–15 cm) racemes and long awns. C. cucullata tends to have crowded shorter whorls and a swollen short-awned sterile hood. C. virgata often has one terminal feathery fan and a different fertile-lemma hair crown. The hybrid between cucullata and verticillata is a real confounder: never certify hybrid status from tier spacing.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Tumble windmillgrass tends to have separated tiers of longer (~5–15 cm) racemes and long awns. C. cucullata tends to have crowded shorter whorls and a swollen short-awned sterile hood. C. virgata often has one terminal feathery fan and a different fertile-lemma hair crown. The hybrid between cucullata and verticillata is a real confounder: never certify hybrid status from tier spacing.

morphology.habit: Perennial windmillgrass with ~10–16 racemes in separated whorls; ripe panicle may detach and tumble.
morphology.spikelets: Fertile lemma awn ~4.8–9 mm; sterile lemma awn ~3.2–7 mm. Upper sterile floret is not a conspicuously swollen round hood.
